Learning Objectives
Identify key risk factors in the perioperative period.
Optimize modifiable risk factors.
Modifiable Preoperative Risk Factors
Emergent situations do not afford adequate time to alter all modifiable risk factors, which
should be considered and optimized in patients undergoing elective procedures.
Other factors, such as patient frailty, age, and medical comorbidities, cannot be modified but
should be considered before elective spine surgery.
The keys to a proper preoperative optimization strategy are to obtain a complete patient
history and perform an adequate physical examination to identify patients with modifiable risk
factors and to connect patients with appropriate resources/services.


Modifiable Preoperative Risk Factors
Medical comorbidities, age, osteoporosis, vitamin D deficiency, nicotine use, steroid use,
obesity, malnutrition, depression, preoperative opiate use, and anemia are considered
risk factors for spine surgery. Spine surgery complications should be thought of as
adverse events that occur within three separate time periods: immediate perioperative
complications, short-term complications (occurring within 90 days postoperatively), and
long-term complications. Immediate perioperative complications include intraoperative
blindness, surgeon error, iatrogenic neurologic injury, dural tears, esophageal injury,
stroke, and cardiac complications. Short-term complications include deep or superficial
wound infection, deep vein thrombosis/venous thromboembolism, impaired wound
healing, implant-related complications, dysphagia, ileus, and urinary retention. Long-
term complications include pseudoarthrosis, infection, implant failure, adjacent segment
degeneration, and persistent back or extremity pain. Several risk modification protocols
have been developed for adults who undergo spine deformity surgery1,2 and can be
used as a guide for all spine surgery. Modifiable risk factors include obesity,
malnutrition, diabetes mellitus, anemia, osteoporosis, nicotine use, and chronic opioid
use (Resource 1). Other factors that may limit surgical outcomes but are not technically
considered risks include depression, anxiety, opioid dependence, and worker’s
compensation status. Other medical risk factors, including coronary artery disease,
congestive heart failure, renal insufficiency, history of cerebrovascular disease, sleep
apnea, compromised hepatic function, and baseline pulmonary insufficiency, should be
optimized preoperatively by the appropriate medical services.
Obesity
Obesity increases the risk of perioperative complications.
Many patients can achieve a healthy weight via a combination of medical resources, such as
consultation with a dietician, evaluation for bariatric surgery, and activity modification.

Obesity
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:40 PM
AAOS | Perioperative Issues
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002022
2/20

The incidence of obesity is increasing3 and presents unique challenges to an elective
spine practice. Patients with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 to 40 kg/m2 are considered
obese, and patients with a BMI greater than 40 kg/m2 are considered morbidly obese.
Patients with obesity have a higher risk for vascular disease, diabetes mellitus, renal
disease, hepatic disease, malignancy, respiratory issues,4 back pain, and intervertebral
disk degeneration.5,6 Obesity is associated with substantial perioperative complications,
including surgical site infection (SSI), pneumonia, cardiac complications, intraoperative
blindness, pressure injuries related to positioning, postoperative wound complications,
and venous thromboembolism.7,8 A large retrospective database study reported that
patients with obesity had a higher complication rate than patients without obesity and
that patients with class III obesity (BMI >40 kg/m2) had a substantially higher risk for
surgical complciations.9 Patients with obesity present technical challenges
intraoperatively, such as difficulty obtaining appropriate imaging studies, difficulty
achieving safe patient positioning, challenging access/exposure, and difficulty achieving
accurate instrumentation, which collectively increase the total surgical time. In addition,
recent evidence suggests that although patients with obesity may experience substantial
improvements after elective spine surgery, their outcome scores are lower than those of
patients without obesity.10 This negative effect on outcomes is associated with a
stepwise progression, with the patients with the greatest obesity having the poorest
outcomes.
Obesity is associated with increased perioperative complications, technical challenges,
and limited improvement but also is a modifiable risk factor. Patients with obesity and
emergent conditions, such as cauda equina or an unstable cervical fracture with a spinal
cord injury, should not be denied surgical treatment. Patients with obesity who wish to
undergo elective procedures should be encouraged to pursue weight loss. The authors
believe that a BMI greater than 40 kg/m2 is a contraindication to elective surgery and
that, ideally, patients undergoing elective surgery should have a BMI less than 35 kg/m2.
Interventions that aid in healthy weight loss include referral to a dietician, a weight
management clinic, bariatric service, and physical therapy for an exercise regimen.
Malnutrition

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002022
3/20

Malnutrition increases perioperative risk by impairing the wound healing process.
Albumin level is the most common method of assessing nutrition status.
Patients are considered malnourished if their albumin level is less than 3.5 g/dL.

Malnutrition
During the course of evaluating patients for elective surgery, surgeons must remember
that patients who are overweight or obese may be malnourished.11 Common laboratory
markers to assess malnutrition include serum albumin level, prealbumin level,
transferrin level, total lymphocyte count, and insulin-like growth factor-1 level.12 In
orthopaedic surgery, patients with a serum albumin level less than 3.5 g/dL and a total
lymphocyte count less than 2,000 cells/mm3 are considered malnourished.13 Elderly
patients who are malnourished have a higher rate of 90-day major medical
complications, a higher 1-year mortality rate, and higher rates of infection and wound
healing complications.14,15 Although nutrition is an important factor to consider in all
patients undergoing spine surgery, special consideration should be given to patients
undergoing complex reconstructive procedures or posterior cervical spine procedures
and patients with active malignancy or infection.16,17 Patients with confirmed nutritional
deficiencies should be referred to a dietician for preoperative and postoperative
optimization.
Diabetes Mellitus
Patients with diabetes mellitus have a higher risk of perioperative mortality, SSI, longer
hospital length of stay, and venous thromboembolism.18,19
The hemoglobin A1c level of patients with diabetes mellitus who wish to undergo elective spine
procedures should be obtained preoperatively. If this value is greater than 7%, then the
patient may have an increased risk for adverse events in the perioperative period.
Perioperative glycemic control is one of the most effective methods to decrease the risk for
adverse events postoperatively, especially SSI.


Diabetes Mellitus
Chronic hyperglycemia has been reported to interfere with neutrophil function.20
Improved glycemic control, as measured by hemoglobin A1c levels, is associated with a
decreased risk of SSI (<7.5% hemoglobin A1c threshold).21 A study found that patients
with a hemoglobin A1c level less than 7.0% had no infections but a 35.3% rate of SSI was
reported in patients with a hemoglobin A1c level higher than 7.0%.22 Other studies,
although not spine specific, have reported an inverse relationship between wound
healing and hemoglobin A1c levels.23,24 In addition, data from the adult reconstruction
literature suggest that patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus have a higher risk of
stroke, urinary tract infection, ileus, and postoperative hemorrhage; higher transfusion
requirements; and higher total hospital costs.25
Surgeons must recognize that perioperative glucose management influences
complication rates. Perioperative hyperglycemia is associated with a higher risk of longer
hospital admission, intensive care unit admission, pneumonia, urinary tract infection,
septicemia, acute renal failure, myocardial infarction, and death.26 One study suggested
that a serum glucose level higher than 150 mg/dL within the first 24 hours
postoperatively is associated with an increased risk for infection.27 This data emphasizes
the importance of strict glucose control in the immediate postoperative setting.
Anemia
Preoperative anemia is associated with a higher risk of intraoperative and postoperative
complications, including 30-day postoperative mortality.28
Preoperative anemia correction may reduce the risk of complications by increasing tolerance
for the surgical procedure.

Anemia

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002022
5/20

Preoperative anemia is associated with comorbidities and may serve as an indication of
a patient’s overall health. A recent retrospective study of patients undergoing elective
posterior spine fusion reported that anemia was associated with a higher risk of
diabetes mellitus, lower albumin levels, and a higher international normalized ratio and
that patients with anemia were more likely to have an American Society of
Anesthesiologists score of 3 or higher.29 The same study also reported a higher
intraoperative risk of stroke and neuromuscular injuries and a higher rate of
complications, including death, blood transfusion, revision surgery, unplanned hospital
readmission, and longer hospital length of stay. Adult reconstruction studies reported
similar findings and suggested that preoperative anemia is associated with increased
blood transfusions, mortality, postoperative pneumonia, and longer hospital length of
stay.30
Correction of anemia may not completely ameliorate the risk of associated
intraoperative and postoperative complications but may optimize a patient’s ability to
tolerate surgery. A patient is considered anemic if the following hemoglobin levels are
discovered preoperatively: females, less than 12 g/dL; males, less than 13 g/dL. Causes of
anemia include nutritional deficiency, undetected gastrointestinal bleeding, iron
deficiency, renal insufficiency, and chronic inflammatory disease.31 Because of the
multiple causes of anemia, the authors recommend collaboration with a patient’s
primary care physician to properly diagnose and manage anemia preoperatively.
Osteoporosis
Poor bone quality is associated with a higher risk of complications.
Preoperative bone health optimization may reduce the incidence and severity of osteoporosis-
related complications.

Osteoporosis
More than 50% of patients older than 50 years who undergo elective spine procedures
have low bone mass or osteoporosis,32 and more than 75% of patients who undergo
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:40 PM
AAOS | Perioperative Issues
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002022
6/20

elective spine procedures have vitamin D deficiency.33,34 Poor bone quality is associated
with an increased risk of instrument-related complications, including cage subsidence,
pedicle screw loosening, and proximal junction failure; an increased rate of
pseudoarthrosis; a higher rate of revision surgery; and increased spondylolisthesis after
laminectomy.35 Low vitamin D levels are associated with slower fusion and an increased
rate of pseudoarthrosis.36
To offset these risks, all patients older than 50 years who are being evaluated for elective
thoracolumbar spine surgery should be screened for osteoporosis.37 Patients without
evidence of compromised bone quality can undergo surgery without additional
intervention. In patients with evidence of compromised bone quality, preoperative
optimization,38 including vitamin D supplementation in combination with
bisphosphonate or anabolic medications, such as teriparatide (authors’ preference),
should be considered. Bisphosphonate and teriparatide therapy support better clinical
and radiographic outcomes with a lower rate of complications.39,40
Nicotine Use
Smoking substantially increases the risk of pseudoarthrosis and SSI.
Smoking may reduce functional outcomes and patient satisfaction postoperatively.
Smoking cessation may decrease the risk of postoperative complications.

Nicotine Use
Although most of the literature focuses on tobacco smoking as a risk factor for
complications in patients undergoing spine surgery, other forms of nicotine delivery,
such as chewing tobacco and vaping, also are clinically relevant. Multiple studies have
reported that smoking is associated with a higher risk of pseudoarthrosis;41 however,
the mechanism is not completely understood. Multiple studies have reported a higher
risk of postoperative SSI and wound healing complications, likely from decreased tissue
oxygenation and dampening of the inflammatory cascade.41

Smoking cessation has been reported to increase the rate of fusion,42 improve patient-
reported outcomes after spine surgery,43 and decrease wound healing complications
and the overall complication rate.44 Although the duration of smoking cessation has not
been definitively established in the spine literature, a meta-analysis of randomized trials
reported that 4 weeks of smoking cessation had a substantially greater treatment effect
than shorter durations of smoking cessation, resulting in a 20% reduction in total
complications.44 The authors recommend smoking cessation for 4 to 6 weeks
preoperatively that is maintained for 3 months after fusion procedures.
Opioid Use
Preoperative opioid use is associated with decreased postoperative functional improvement,
an increased risk of revision surgery, and longer hospital length of stay postoperatively.
The risk of sustained prescription opioid use is low for individuals not taking opioid
medications at the time of surgery.

Opioid Use
Although opioids are a short-term nonsurgical treatment modality for the management
of chronic low back pain,45 many patients presenting to an elective spine practice are
being treated via chronic opioid therapy. Although recent research had shown that the
risk of sustained prescription opioid use is low for individuals not taking opioid
medications at the time of surgery, patients who regularly take opioids at the time of
surgery have an increased risk for adverse postoperative events. A 2007 study suggested
that approximately 20% of patients presenting to an elective spine practice were opioid
dependent.46 Chronic opioid use is counterproductive because it is associated with
increased levels of baseline pain via a sensitization process referred to as opioid-induced
hyperalgesia.47 A 2020 systematic review of more than 45 studies reported that
preoperative opioid use is substantially associated with higher inpatient and
postoperative opioid use, poorer patient-reported and functional outcomes, increased
hospital length of stay, increased medical costs, 90-day readmission, and increased
complication rates.48 In the adult reconstruction literature, preoperative opioid

reduction by at least 50% has been reported to improve postoperative patient outcomes
to a level similar to those of opioid-naïve patients.49
These findings emphasize the importance of having honest discussions with patients
about their preoperative opioid use and facilitating reduction or cessation of these
medications. Ideally, patients should be opioid free or taking less than 10 mg of
morphine equivalents per day (10 mg of hydrocodone or 5 mg of oxycodone per day)
preoperatively. A multidisciplinary approach with the patient’s primary care provider, a
pain management service, and a pain psychiatric service may help patients safely
achieve opioid independence. Recently available web-based applications based on
machine learning algorithms (
https://sorg-apps.shinyapps.io/lumbaropioidnaive) may help identify patients at risk for
extended opioid use after lumbar spine surgery.50 In addition, tools such as the Stopping
Opioids after Surgery score have been validated in patients undergoing cervical and
lumbar spine surgery and may facilitate decisions regarding postoperative pain control.
Procedure-Specific Risk Factors
Procedure-specific risk factors should be considered in selection of the optimal strategy to
manage spinal disorders.
The ability of a patient to tolerate procedure-related complications must be considered to
decrease risk exposure.

Procedure-Specific Risk Factors
The invasiveness and associated morbidity of spine procedures exists on a spectrum.
The authors propose the stratification of spine procedures as low risk, medium risk, and
high risk. Low-risk procedures include lumbar microdiskectomy, lumbar laminectomy of
two levels or less without fusion, anterior cervical diskectomy and fusion, and anterior
cervical diskectomy and arthroplasty. Medium-risk procedures include anterior cervical
corpectomy and fusion; cervical laminoplasty; cervical laminectomy and fusion; and

lumbar spine fusion of less than three levels, including anterior lumbar interbody fusion,
transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion, and lateral lumbar interbody fusion. High-risk
procedures include lumbar spine fusion of three or more levels; deformity procedures;
procedures to manage tumors, infections, trauma; and revision procedures.
Preoperative and Inpatient Protocols
Postoperative Pain Management
Sustained postoperative opioid use is associated with complications that may delay discharge
and impede recovery after spine surgery.
Implementation of a multimodal pain strategy may provide adequate pain control and
minimize the complications associated with narcotic pain medications. 

Postoperative Pain Management
Spine surgery may generate considerable pain in the immediate postoperative period.
Uncontrolled postoperative pain increase a patient’s risk for mobility-associated
complications, such as pneumonia and venous thromboembolism, whereas satisfactory
pain control may facilitate earlier discharge and better surgical outcomes.51 Narcotic
pain medications are important in postoperative pain control but are associated with
complications, such as respiratory depression, altered mental status, ileus, urinary
retention, and longer hospital length of stay.52 Multimodal pain control pathways involve
the use of combinations of other medications to minimize postoperative narcotic use
and provide adequate pain control.
A preoperative discussion about postoperative pain management (pain plan) is
important to help set patient expectations, involve patients in the decision-making
process, and facilitate a consistent implementation strategy. Reducing preoperative
opioid consumption also facilitates better postoperative pain control. Multimodal pain
pathways are likely institutionally dependent; however, commonly used medications
include short-term NSAIDs (possible increased risk of nonunion with high-dose
ketorolac), neuromodulatory agents (gabapentin/pregabalin), local anesthesia infiltration

of the surgical site intraoperatively, acetaminophen, dexamethasone, and muscle
relaxers.53
Preoperative Protocols to Reduce SSI
Nicotine cessation, nutrition optimization, glucose control, and healthy body weight may
decrease the risk of SSI.
Preoperative nasal swabs also may reduce the risk of SSI by identifying methicillin-sensitive
Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA) carriers. This allows for
preoperative decolonization and appropriate selection of perioperative antibiotic agents.

Preoperative Protocols to Reduce SSI
SSIs are associated with increased morbidity, increased costs, and poorer patient-
reported outcomes.54,55 Optimization of modifiable risk factors may facilitate lower
infection rates. Adhering to sterile technique and meticulous wound closure also
decreases the risk of SSI and wound healing complications. Other interventions, such as
preoperative nasal swabs, appropriate selection of perioperative antibiotic agents, and
vancomycin powder, have been reported to reduce SSI.
The incidence of methicillin-sensitive S aureus and MRSA varies in different patient
populations. A level III study of 7,019 patients undergoing elective orthopaedic surgery
reported a 22.6% incidence of S aureus carriers and a 4.4% incidence of MRSA via nasal
swabs.56 Patients with positive swabs for methicillin-sensitive S aureus or MRSA were
prescribed a course of intranasal mupirocin and a daily chlorhexidine shower wash for 5
days preoperatively. Patients positive for MRSA also were administered intravenous
vancomycin in addition to standard preoperative antibiotic agents. This combination
substantially reduced the incidence of SSI compared with a historical control. Other
studies have demonstrated a reduction in SSIs via a similar protocol.57,58
First- or third-generation cephalosporins are the perioperative antibiotic agents most
commonly used in patients without a confirmed history of penicillin or cephalosporin

anaphylaxis. Vancomycin or clindamycin can be used in patients with a true allergy to
penicillin or cephalosporins. Perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis via a single
preoperative dose of cefuroxime has been reported to decrease the incidence of SSI
(1.3% versus 2.8%) and the incidence of spondylodiscitis or epidural abscess (zero versus
1.4%) in patients undergoing lumbar diskectomy.59 Multiple studies have demonstrated
no additional benefit of multiple doses of perioperative antibiotic agents.60,61
Intrawound vancomycin also has been reported to reduce the incidence of SSI. A recent
meta-analysis of 27 studies that included 17,321 patients reported a substantial
reduction in the incidence of SSI in patients undergoing instrumentation but not in
patients undergoing deformity or uninstrumented procedures.62 A recent systematic
review suggested that vancomycin powder substantially decreases the risk of SSI but
does not increase the risk of gram-negative infections, which was previously
suggested.63
Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring
The use of intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring (IONM) is indicated in spinal cord level
deformity procedures with correction, in patients with a spinal cord level traumatic injury, in
the reduction of high-grade spondylolisthesis, in patients with a tumor, and in longer surgical
procedures in which peripheral nerve injuries may result from patient positioning.
If IONM is used, a combination of somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEPs) and motor-evoked
potentials (MEPs) is optimal.

Intraoperative Neurophysiologic Monitoring
IONM is a blanket-term that includes several modalities, such SSEPs, MEPs, and
spontaneous/triggered electromyography.64 SSEPs involve the use of signal averaging to
assess function of the dorsal columns, which may create delays in detecting acute spinal
cord injury. A 50% amplitude decrease with a 10% latency increase is associated with a
potential spinal cord injury. SSEP readings are sensitive to changes in blood pressure
and to anesthesia; therefore, SSEPs not specific for neurologic injury. MEPs provide a

9/3/26, 5:40 PM
AAOS | Perioperative Issues
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002022
12/20

real-time measure of the descending corticospinal tracts, nerve roots, and peripheral
nerves and can be used to immediately detect potential neurologic injury.
The use of IONM has increased;65 however, whether IONM influences the incidence of
neurologic injury in routine elective procedures has not been definitively established. A
2018 systematic review was unable to demonstrate that IONM led to a lower incidence
of perioperative neurologic injuries, with the exception of a trend toward lower rates of
neurologic injury in patients who underwent intramedullary tumor procedures.66
Another database study of 9,957 patients suggested that the routine use of IONM in
patients without spinal deformity who underwent posterior lumbar spine fusion did not
decrease the risk of intraoperative neurologic complications.67
The routine use of IONM is controversial and its implementation should be guided by the
complexity of the surgical procedure and the risk of potential neurologic injury. If IONM
is used, a combination of SSEPs and MEPs should be implemented to optimize sensitivity
and specificity.68 In a review of more than 100,000 cases from a surgical registry, the
sensitivity of IONM for the detection of new spinal cord injury during corrective
deformity procedures was 43%;69 however, because of the complexity of these
procedures, the routine use of IONM should be considered. The literature supports the
use of IONM for tumor surgery, the management of spinal cord level fracture-
dislocations, and the reduction of high-grade spondylolisthesis.70-72
